qs.q: Which of the following groups of Glossina species is insignificant in the transmission of Trypanosoma brucei rhodesiense?
qs.e: The G. fuscipes group (e.g., G. tachinoides, G. fuscipes) are primarily vectors of Trypanosoma brucei gambiense (West African sleeping sickness) and are typically found in riparian vegetation. G. pallidipes and G. longipennis are more associated with G. brucei rhodesiense transmission, found in woodland and savannah habitats. The G. palpalis group, while also associated with Gambiense, can play a role in Rhodesiense

qs.q: Presence of triatomine bugs (kissing bugs) can predispose the population to Chagas disease, caused by the parasite Trypanosoma cruzi.
qs.e: Triatomine bugs, also known as kissing bugs, are the vectors for Trypanosoma cruzi, the parasite that causes Chagas disease. They often bite sleeping humans and defecate near the bite wound; the parasite is then introduced into the body when the feces are rubbed into the bite or mucous membranes.

ai.subject: Microbiology & immunology
ai.summary: Trypanosoma are protozoan parasites transmitted by insects that cause African sleeping sickness and Chagas disease. They invade blood, tissue and the nervous system, leading to systemic and cardiac complications.

sections.p: Trypanosoma are flagellated protozoa of the order Kinetoplastida. Two species are clinically important: T. brucei (subspecies gambiense and rhodesiense) causing African trypanosomiasis, and T. cruzi causing American trypanosomiasis (Chagas disease).
b: Transmitted by tsetse flies (T. brucei) or triatomine bugs (T. cruzi)
Endemic in sub‑Saharan Africa and Latin America

sections.p: They possess a kinetoplast DNA, a single mitochondrion, and a flagellum that aids motility and immune evasion through antigenic variation (VSG coat).
b: Intracellular amastigotes (T. cruzi) hide in muscle and nerve cells

sections.p: T. brucei is acquired when a tsetse fly bites a host, injecting metacyclic trypomastigotes that multiply in blood and lymph. T. cruzi is transmitted when a triatomine bug defecates on skin; metacyclic trypomastigotes enter through mucosa or breaks, become intracellular amastigotes, then release trypomastigotes into blood.
b: Vector control is key in low‑resource settings
Oral transmission of T. cruzi via contaminated food occurs in outbreaks

sections.p: African sleeping sickness presents in two stages: early haemolymphatic (fever, headache, lymphadenopathy) and late meningo‑encephalitic (sleep disturbance, neuropsychiatric signs). Chagas disease has acute phase (fever, chagoma, myocarditis) and chronic phase (cardiomyopathy, megacolon, arrhythmias).
b: Co‑infection with HIV, malaria or TB worsens outcomes

sections.p: Microscopy, serology and molecular tests are used depending on stage and resource availability.
b: If microscopy unavailable, rely on serology for chronic Chagas and clinical picture for African trypanosomiasis

t.b: Detects parasites in early African trypanosomiasis; positive means active infection
Confirms late-stage disease; elevated white cells/protein plus parasites indicates CNS involvement

t.a: Serology (ELISA, indirect immunofluorescence) for T. cruzi
t.b: Positive in chronic Chagas; helps when parasites are not seen
Highly sensitive; useful when microscopy unavailable or for treatment monitoring

sections.p: Therapy is stage‑specific. Early African trypanosomiasis uses pentamidine (T. b. gambiense) or suramin (T. b. rhodesiense). Late stage requires melarsoprol or nifurtimox‑eflornithine combination. Chagas acute phase uses benznidazole; chronic phase treatment is limited to benznidazole or nifurtimox in selected patients.
b: Pentamidine/Suramin act on bloodstream trypomastigotes; avoid in renal failure
Melarsoprol crosses BBB but causes severe encephalopathy; reserve for late T. b. rhodesiense
Benznidazole targets intracellular amastigotes; monitor for dermatitis and neuropathy

sections.p: Key points to remember for exams and clinical practice.
b: African trypanosomiasis: early stage = fever + lymphadenopathy; late stage = sleep disturbance + CSF parasites
Chagas chronic disease: cardiomyopathy with apical aneurysm, megacolon, and positive serology
Antigenic variation explains why patients can have relapsing parasitemia despite immune response

whenToSeekHelp: Neurological deterioration (coma, seizures) in sleeping sickness
Acute heart failure or severe arrhythmia in Chagas disease
Persistent fever with lymphadenopathy in a traveler from endemic area

faq.q: Why does sleeping sickness cause daytime sleepiness?
faq.a: Parasites invade the hypothalamus, disrupting circadian regulation and causing somnolence.

faq.q: Can Chagas disease be cured in the chronic phase?
faq.a: Treatment may reduce parasite load and slow cardiac damage, but complete cure is uncommon.

faq.q: What is the role of vector control?
faq.a: Eliminating tsetse flies and triatomine bugs reduces transmission and is the most sustainable prevention in low‑resource settings.
